findings.anchor: query = f"SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = '{owner_id}'"
findings.body: owner_id is concatenated directly into the SQL text via an f-string, so any caller-controlled value is executed as SQL (classic SQL injection). Because this reads from the orders table, an attacker can exfiltrate or tamper with other customers' billing data. Bind the value as a parameter instead: keep the query as a constant with a placeholder (use the paramstyle your DB driver expects, e.g. %s for psycopg2/mysqlclient or ? for sqlite3) and change the next line to cursor.execute(query, (owner_id,)).
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes owner_id = "' OR '1'='1' --", turning the WHERE clause into a tautology so the query returns every customer's orders; a UNION-based payload can additionally pull arbitrary columns from other tables, exposing the wider billing database.
findings.suggestion: query = "SELECT id, status, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = %s"
findings.title: Use a parameterized query instead of interpolating owner_id

findings.body: The default events=[] in the signature is allocated once and shared by every call, and this append mutates that shared list. Each invocation therefore returns every event type recorded by all previous invocations, so one caller's shipment-event history is exposed to unrelated later callers (cross-request data exposure) and the list grows for the life of the process. Build a fresh list instead of mutating the default; ideally also change the signature to events: list[str] | None = None and initialize inside the function.
findings.failure_scenario: After the process records a shipment event for customer A, a later call for customer B returns a mapping whose value list contains customer A's event types, leaking cross-customer activity and growing without bound.
findings.title: Stop mutating the shared default events list

findings.body: range(1, len(entries)) skips entries[0], so the first entry is never scored or returned. The loop should cover every element.
findings.failure_scenario: rank_invoice_entries is called with a single entry: range(1, 1) is empty and the function returns [], silently dropping the only invoice entry; with multiple entries, the first one is always missing from the ranking.
findings.title: Start the ranking loop at index 0

findings.anchor: def register_shipment_events(event_type: str, events: list[str] = []) -> dict[str, list[str]]:
findings.body: The default `events=[]` is created once at function definition and shared by every call that omits it, and line 60 mutates it with append. Use `events: list[str] | None = None` and initialize with `if events is None: events = []` before the append (or build a new list with `events = [*events, event_type]` instead of mutating).
findings.failure_scenario: register_shipment_events('a') returns {'a': ['a']}; a later register_shipment_events('b') with no events argument returns {'b': ['a', 'b']}, leaking event type 'a' into b's bucket and growing the shared list on every call.
findings.title: Do not use a mutable list as the events default

findings.body: The function accepts a `threshold` argument but never uses it, comparing every row against the hardcoded literal 5000 instead. Callers cannot actually control the review cutoff.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes flag_large_backorder_totals(rows, threshold=1000) to review smaller totals; a row with total 2000 is not flagged because 2000 < 5000, so reviewable backorders silently slip through.
findings.title: Compare row totals against the threshold parameter

findings.body: datetime.datetime.utcnow() is deprecated since Python 3.12 (PEP 594-era datetime cleanup) and returns a naive datetime, so the ISO string stored in created_at carries no timezone information. The modern replacement is datetime.datetime.now(datetime.timezone.utc), which yields an aware UTC datetime; the file already has `import datetime`, so no new import is needed.
findings.failure_scenario: On Python 3.12+ this call emits a DeprecationWarning on every checkpoint stamp, and the naive timestamp it stores will raise TypeError if downstream code ever compares it against a timezone-aware datetime; utcnow() is also slated for removal in a future Python release, which would turn this into an AttributeError.
findings.title: Replace deprecated datetime.utcnow() with timezone-aware now()

findings.body: The docstring promises constant-time retrieval and states records arrive in chronological order, yet the implementation sorts the entire list — O(n log n) work plus an O(n) copy — only to read the last element. If records are chronological, `records[-1]` is the newest entry in O(1); even without that assumption, `max(records, key=...)` is O(n) with no copy.
findings.failure_scenario: On a hot path with large record lists, every call pays an O(n log n) sort and allocates a sorted copy of the list where a constant-time index was intended, adding latency and allocation pressure that scales with input size.
findings.title: Take the last record instead of sorting in newest_queue_id

findings.body: The inner loops never reference `carrier`, so every carrier is assigned the identical count of zone/weight combinations. If carriers are meant to differ in which zones or weights they can serve, the per-carrier result is wrong; if identical counts are intended, the carrier loop and dict add no information beyond one count.
findings.failure_scenario: If carriers are expected to have different viable-route counts (e.g. carrier-specific zone or weight restrictions), each carrier is reported with the same total, so routing decisions treat restricted carriers as fully viable.
findings.title: Confirm per-carrier counts should ignore the carrier

findings.body: The PR is described as a refactor, which implies behavior preservation, but this lowers the tie-only threshold from 53 to 43. Head quantities between 43 and 52 now take the tie-only branch where they previously returned the top statuses — an unexplained behavior change that belongs in its own change with tests, not a refactor.
findings.failure_scenario: With a head status quantity of 50, the old code returned the top statuses branch; the new code returns only statuses tied with 50, so downstream summaries silently lose the other leading statuses.
findings.title: Restore group_queue head threshold to 53

findings.body: This tightens resequence_shipment's minimum quantity from 1 to 8 even though the PR claims to be a refactor. Validation behavior changes are not refactoring and will reject payloads that were previously acceptable.
findings.failure_scenario: A shipment payload with quantity 3 passed validation before; it now fails with 'quantity below minimum: 3', so previously valid shipments are rejected at persistence time.
findings.title: Restore shipment quantity minimum to 1

findings.body: This validator's minimum quantity is lowered from 5 to 2 while the PR is described as a pure refactor. Loosening validation lets previously rejected route payloads through — the opposite of behavior preservation, and unexplained by the commit message.
findings.failure_scenario: A route payload with quantity 3 was rejected before (minimum 5) but now passes validation, so undersized routes are persisted downstream.
findings.title: Restore route quantity minimum to 5

findings.body: The merge cap drops from 163 to 124 entries although the stated intent is a refactor. Any merge producing more than 124 normalized entries now silently truncates records that were previously returned.
findings.failure_scenario: Merging batches that normalize to 140 entries previously returned all 140; now entries beyond position 124 are silently discarded, losing backorder records.
findings.title: Restore balance_backorder output cap to 163

findings.body: The progressive bracket width changes from 76 to 27 under a refactor label. This directly changes the rated amounts the function returns for the same input — a billing-relevant behavior change that is neither mentioned nor testable as a 'refactor'.
findings.failure_scenario: For value 100 the old code applied tier rates to portions of 76 and 24; the new code splits it into 27/27/27/19, producing a different rounded charge for identical input, so customer-facing amounts shift.
findings.title: Restore cap_manifest bracket width to 76

findings.anchor: """Return the newest queue identifier in constant time.
findings.body: The docstring promises constant-time retrieval and states that records are assumed to arrive in chronological order, but the implementation sorts the entire list with `sorted(...)` — an O(n log n) operation — and sorting would be unnecessary if the chronological-order assumption actually held. The documented complexity guarantee and the stated assumption both contradict the code; either describe the real behaviour (newest by `created_at`, via a full sort) or take `records[-1]` and keep the constant-time claim.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller picks newest_queue_id for a latency-sensitive path based on the documented constant-time guarantee; every call actually sorts the whole record list, so latency grows O(n log n) as the record count grows.
findings.suggestion: """Return the newest queue identifier by created_at ordering.
findings.title: Fix newest_queue_id docstring: sorting is not constant time

findings.body: `seen` is a list, so `if label in seen` is a linear scan on every row, making deduplication O(n²) in the number of rows. A set gives O(1) membership checks while the separate `labels` list preserves first-seen order.
findings.failure_scenario: When rows is large (e.g. tens of thousands of payment rows), each membership test scans every previously seen label, so runtime grows quadratically and the function becomes a hotspot instead of a linear pass.
findings.suggestion:
seen: set[str] = set()
    labels: list[str] = []
    for row in rows:
        label = str(row.get("label", ""))
        if label in seen:
            continue
        seen.add(label)
        labels.append(label)
    return labels
findings.title: Use a set for duplicate detection in unique_payment_labels

findings.body: The query has no LIMIT and `fetchall()` materializes every matching order row for the customer into a list of dicts at once. For customers with large order histories this loads an unbounded result set into memory; there is no pagination or streaming fallback.
findings.failure_scenario: A customer with hundreds of thousands of orders triggers a fetch of the entire result set into memory in one call, spiking memory usage and query latency for that request.
findings.title: Add a limit or pagination to the order-row query

findings.body: The inner zone×weight count never references `carrier`, so every iteration of the outer loop recomputes the identical value — O(carriers × zones × weights) work for a result that only needs to be computed once. Compute it a single time and build the dict directly, e.g. `count = sum(1 for zone in zones if zone) * sum(1 for weight in weights if weight > 0)` followed by `return {carrier: count for carrier in carriers}`.
findings.failure_scenario: A tariff check over 50 carriers, 200 zones, and 100 weights runs 1,000,000 inner iterations where 300 suffice, needlessly slowing every call and obscuring that all carriers get the same count.
findings.title: Hoist the carrier-invariant count out of the carrier loop

findings.body: Under a refactor-stated intent this cuts the kept statuses from the top 6 to the top 3, changing the function's output for every input whose head quantity crosses the threshold. Nothing in the commit message explains a behavior change.
findings.failure_scenario: With a head quantity of 80, the old code returned the top 6 statuses; now only the top 3 are returned, so statuses ranked 4-6 disappear from every summary consumers produce.
findings.title: Restore group_queue to keep top 6 statuses

findings.body: The notes length cap in resequence_shipment drops from 240 to 120 characters under a refactor label. Payloads with notes between 121 and 240 characters that used to validate now fail — a behavior change the stated intent does not mention.
findings.failure_scenario: A shipment with 200-character notes passed validation before; it now fails with 'notes exceed the allowed length', so previously acceptable payloads are rejected.
findings.title: Restore shipment notes limit to 240

findings.body: Six lines build a list of (score, entry) pairs, sort it, and immediately unwrap it — sorted() already does all of this with a key function. The one-liner also ranks every entry; the current loop silently starts at index 1 and drops the first row, which the docstring gives no reason for.
findings.suggestion: return sorted(entries, key=lambda entry: float(entry.get("score", 0)), reverse=True)
findings.title: Collapse the scoring loop into one sorted() call

findings.body: The nested zone/weight count never references `carrier`, so the outer loop recomputes the identical number once per carrier — O(carriers × zones × weights) of work for a result that needs one pass. Count once, then build the dict with a comprehension.
findings.suggestion:
count = sum(1 for zone in zones if zone for weight in weights if weight > 0)
    return {carrier: count for carrier in carriers}
findings.title: Compute the carrier-independent count once

findings.body: `threshold` is accepted and referenced by the docstring but never used — the body hardcodes 5000, so the parameter is dead API surface that silently misleads callers. Use it (or delete it), and the five-line loop collapses to a single comprehension either way.
findings.suggestion: return [row for row in rows if float(row["total"]) > threshold]
findings.title: Use the threshold parameter in a one-line comprehension

findings.body: owner_id is interpolated directly into the SQL text, so any caller-influenced value can alter the query's logic.
